hints: Look closely at Fig. 1.3 and trace the flow - tyrosine is changed into X, and then X can go two ways to make either light brown or black pigment.
walkthrough:
Follow the Pathway in the Melanocyte**
Tyrosine is the starting amino acid in melanocytes. It is converted by the enzyme tyrosinase into an intermediate, substance X, which is then converted onward into either phaeomelanin when MC1R is not activated or eumelanin when MC1R is activated.

Name the Intermediate**
That common intermediate between tyrosine and the two melanins is DOPA, which is quickly converted to dopaquinone. Either name is accepted, as both are the direct product before the branch point.

hints: Think about how a signal is passed on inside the cell after a receptor like MC1R in the cell surface membrane is triggered - a small soluble molecule is made to relay the message.
walkthrough:
Recall How Receptors Signal Inside**
MC1R is a cell surface membrane receptor. When it is activated by a signal outside, it cannot act directly on enzymes deep in the cell, so it triggers production of a small molecule inside the cytoplasm to carry the message onward.

Pick the Classic Example**
The most common second messenger made in this type of signalling is cyclic AMP, abbreviated cAMP, formed from ATP by adenyl cyclase.

hints: Start from the block in Fig. 1.3 - if substance X is never made, what happens to production of both phaeomelanin and eumelanin in skin, hair and eyes?
Link lack of pigment to the visible human condition - think about skin and hair colour, eye colour appearance, and problems with vision in bright light.
walkthrough:
Connect the Mutation to No Pigment**
The TYR gene codes for tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes substance X from tyrosine. If X is not produced, neither phaeomelanin nor eumelanin can be made, so melanocytes make no melanin pigment at all.

Describe the Visible Phenotype**
This is albinism. Without melanin the skin is very pale and hair is white. The irises look red or pink because with no pigment you see blood vessels through them, and vision is poor with sensitivity to light and jerky eye movements because melanin is needed for normal eye development and protection.
Final answer: Person has albinism; very pale skin / white hair due to no melanin pigment; red / pink irises; poor vision / sensitive to light.

hints: Compare the two breeding observations - light brown x light brown always breeds true, but black x black can produce light brown young. Which phenotype must be hiding the other allele?
Choose clear allele symbols, for example B for the black allele and b for the light brown allele, and state which is dominant and which is recessive.
To get both colours from two black parents, what must the genotype of each black parent be so they can both pass on the hidden light brown allele?
Set out a Punnett square with gametes B and b from each parent and read off the expected genotype ratio and matching phenotype ratio.
walkthrough:
Work Out Dominant and Recessive**
Light brown x light brown gives only light brown, so light brown breeds true and must be homozygous recessive. Black x black can give light brown young, so black parents must be carrying a hidden light brown allele. That means black is dominant to light brown.

Define Symbols and Parental Genotypes**
Let B = allele for black fur, dominant, and b = allele for light brown fur, recessive. The two black parents that produce mixed offspring must both be heterozygous: Bb x Bb. Each parent makes gametes B and b by meiosis.

Complete the Punnett Square**
Put B, b down one side and B, b across the top:
$$ \begin{array}{c|cc} & B & b \\ \hline B & BB & Bb \\ b & Bb & bb \end{array} $$
Offspring genotypes are $BB$, $Bb$, $Bb$, $bb$ in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio.

Translate to Phenotypes**
$BB$ and $Bb$ all make eumelanin because the dominant B allele is present, so they have black fur. Only $bb$ lacks B and has light brown fur. This gives a 3 black : 1 light brown phenotype ratio, which explains how two black jaguars can have some black and some light brown cubs.
Final answer: Let B = black fur (dominant), b = light brown fur (recessive); parents: Bb x Bb; gametes: B, b x B, b; offspring genotypes: BB, Bb, Bb, bb; offspring phenotypes: 3 black : 1 light brown
